title: Intend Introduces User-Serviceable Elevator Dropper Post
content:
Intend designs and manufactures jewelry-quality mountain bike components in Freiburg, Germany. Their products are somehow both space-aged and understated. But there’s always some unique tech inside that makes Intend parts more than mere fashion statements. That’s especially true of the new Intend Elevator dropper post.

The Intend Elevator chassis is hand-assembled by Intend using parts made by a small manufacturing partner in Taiwan. But there’s nothing off-the-shelf in the design, and they cut no corners. The upper tube and saddle clamp are one single forged and finished part. And then inside the tube, things get interesting.

Instead of leaving the bottom of the post open for displaced air to pass as the post moves, Intend sealed it off to create what they’re calling “Safe Space.” This does a few things. It increases the natural ramp-up in air pressure as you drop, which Intend claims eases the action of compressing the post. Instead of having to deliberately position your hips to gently push your saddle to full compression, you can just drop your body weight onto it with no hard bottom-out. It makes sense, though we haven’t had an opportunity to try it.

Intend Elevator Quick Hits

  • Fully sealed lower chamber adds progression for softer bottom-outs
  • Oil-bath lubrication provides smoother action and longer service life than traditional grease
  • Natural anodized, one-piece upper tube
  • Fully user-serviceable, including cartridge
  • Assembled in-house by hand in Freiburg, Germany
  • Component parts manufactured in Taiwan
  • 31,6mm only, at time of publishing
  • 190mm stroke, adjustable in 10mm steps
  • 276mm insertion depth (plus 25mm cable attachment) for all lengths
  • Elevator Boy remote lever with Matchmaker mount and quick-release cable sold separately for €66.39 / $77
  • €318.49 / $368, plus import duties and €100.00 / $116 to ship to the US.

The other benefit to Safe Space is that the system is fully sealed, just like a suspension fork. And just like a suspension fork, it can be lubricated with an oil bath instead of a grease smear. Oil isn’t static like grease, and will naturally circulate inside the post to keep things running smooth for a long, long time. They haven’t published recommended service intervals yet, but they claim this post can go much farther than traditional posts between disassembly and cleaning.

The internals still work like a traditional dropper, by locking and unlocking fluid as it passes between chambers. But those internals are more robust than most, with IGUS bushings that get a generous overlap for straighter, smoother, longer-lasting action. It self-bleeds at every top-out, so air ingress will never leave it feeling soft. But if it ever does need attention, the cartridge is fully user-serviceable.

The post is internally adjustable from 190 mm down to 120 mm in 10 mm increments. That means there’s only one chassis, so riders who may be stretching to fit shorter posts will need deep enough frame insertion to accommodate the 273mm lower half, plus 25mm of cable mechanism. On the note of frame insertion, the Elevator currently only comes in a 31.6mm diameter. Sort of a weird choice, since you could shim up a 30.9 post. And 190 mm is a bit short for a max length in 2026. But Intend hopes to evolve the post over time and introduce more lengths and more diameters.

While the Elevator works with most remote levers, Intend also made their own. The Elevator Boy uses a Matchmaker interface and runs on sealed cartridge bearings. We’ve seen that before. What we haven’t seen is its quick-release cable attachment. Not unlike an old V-brake lever, you can unhook both cable and housing from the remote. This eliminates the need to remove the lever when pulling out the post, and should make it easier to cut the cable to length. And the Elevator Boy is of course compatible with any modern cable-actuated dropper.

Tariffs are still in turmoil as we publish this, but the Elevator dropper on its own goes for €318.49 or about $368 and the Elevator Boy remote is €66.39 or about $77. Intend charges a flat rate of €100.00 or about $116 to ship to the US.
